items.title: Scheduler correctness blockers: no self-mutation, typed permission provenance
items.value: Recurring jobs stop pausing themselves: automatic policy allows no longer read as human one-time consent, scheduled runs lose scheduler mutation tools (surface + signed host rejection), and scheduler mutations ask in auto mode per decision 0058.
acceptance_criteria: recurring job stays active after runs containing auto_classifier / cached_classifier_verdict / trusted_root_grant / birthright / deterministic_read_only / reviewed_rule allows; pauses only on explicit human one-time consent
scheduled runs mount only scheduler read tools; forged mutation IPC from a scheduled source is host-rejected via signed sourceJobId/sourceRunId/sourceRunKind
scheduler mutation+delete tools classify ask in normal auto mode (reads stay birthright); the tests requiring auto-approval are corrected
scheduled prompt drops the self-edit instruction and states the no-mutation control policy; runs report proposedJobChange in outcomes
items.outcome: Recurring jobs no longer pause themselves: the runtime now distinguishes automatic policy approvals from genuine human one-time consent, and only the latter pauses a job — with every automatic path regression-tested and ambiguous records treated safely. Scheduled runs also lost the ability to edit their own future: the six scheduler mutation tools are gone from unattended runs at two independent layers (the tool list they see, and a host-side check they cannot forge because it keys on values only the host mints), scheduler changes now ask a human in auto mode as decision 0058 always required, and every request carries signed source-run provenance for auditing. The self-pausing loop that hit the lead-maintenance job is closed at all four of its causes.

items.title: Approval & setup-notification UX: explicit scope, no contradictory cards, match-vs-grant diagnosis
items.value: Kills the confusion that made the pause loop undiagnosable: approvals say whether they are one-time or durable (and confirm 'will ask again next run'), a run that recovers never sends a green Completed card and an orange Setup-needed card as peers, and 'granted but pattern did not match' reads differently from 'not granted' with the attempted-vs-approved diff shown.
acceptance_criteria: approval prompts offer explicit scope (Allow once / Allow for future / Deny — the locked set) with read-only tools defaulting to the durable option; an Allow-once confirmation states 'Approved for this run only; it will ask again next run'

when a run completes after a blocked-but-degraded step, the setup card is folded into the completion ('Completed with limits' + degraded line) or suppressed in favor of a completion badge — never two contradictory peer cards
permission denials distinguish not-granted from granted-but-unmatched, showing the approved pattern vs the attempted command
same job + same tool asked more than twice escalates the copy with the ask count and a permanent-approval offer
items.outcome: Permission and job notifications now tell the truth plainly. Approving something once says so — 'Approved for this run only; future runs will need approval again' — instead of leaving you to discover the difference later. A job that finishes despite a blocked step sends ONE card ('Completed with limits', naming what degraded and every one-time approval) instead of a green Completed and an orange Setup-needed contradicting each other, and no path can leave a paused job silent. A command blocked because its shape didn't match shows the approved pattern next to what was attempted — ending the 'was it even granted?' guessing from the incident. And a repeating permission prompt now says how many times you've approved it and over how many days, offering to make it permanent.

items.title: Job definition revision fencing: concurrent edits survive finalization

items.title: Actionable job cards: approve-from-card, full setup story, visible recovery, provider parity
items.value: The buttonless 'Setup needed' card gains an approve-this-requirement affordance that settles through the existing permission path on every provider (and survives durable delivery); setup cards say which step broke and whether the run died or degraded, listing every blocker; durable-grant auto-resume drains past 100 and tells the job's conversation; lifecycle bubbles retire on crash/dead-letter/stale-lease exits; discord/teams reach action parity or degrade visibly to text.
acceptance_criteria: setup cards carry an approve-this-requirement affordance (locked option semantics, settling through the existing permission-authorization path — no new grant path) rendered and parseable on slack, telegram, discord and teams, and preserved through the durable enqueue payload
setup cards state the failed action, the triggering step, died-vs-degraded, and every distinct blocker (or count + expand); bare tool ids never shown
durable-grant recovery paginates until drained and emits a route-scoped resumed/queued receipt for each affected job (bounded aggregate allowed)
lifecycle/progress messages are retired or replaced on ALL terminal exits including crash, dead-letter and stale-lease, with per-exit-path tests
provider-neutral card actions render on every supported channel or degrade visibly to text — no silently dropped affordances
items.outcome: Scheduled-job cards are now actionable. When a job pauses for missing access it raises the real permission prompt (Allow for future / Deny) built from the job's stored requirement, settled through the existing durable permission path with a fingerprint fence; setup cards say what failed, at which step, whether the run died or degraded, and list every blocker in plain words; Discord and Teams reach button parity with Slack/Telegram. Durable-grant recovery drains all paused jobs (the 100-cap is gone) with a fail-open 'resumed' receipt per job, and stale 'running' bubbles retire on every terminal exit without blocking execution. Shipped over 11 stages; verify.py caught two full-suite regressions we then fixed. Three bounded, user-revocable residuals are tracked as deferrals (D-0044/45/46).

items.title: Autonomous jobs pause-and-ask on tool denial instead of silently degrading
items.value: A scheduled job that hits a tool it isn't granted stops silently substituting another tool (e.g. Browser) and burning the run. The denial is terminal: a grantable one pauses the job and raises the approval card naming the tool (one tap grants it, and for an under-declared tool the same tap adds it to the job's requirements), then the job retries; a non-grantable one ends with a legible instruction card. A job waiting for approval never times out or dead-letters; a late grant just reruns it fresh.
acceptance_criteria: an autonomous-job tool denial is terminal and never results in silent continuation with another tool

a grantable denial pauses the job and raises the SCHED-4B approval card naming the specific tool; approving grants the agent and, for an under-declared tool, also adds it to the job's access_requirements (human-initiated, 0106-consistent), then the job retries
a non-grantable denial (locked/fixed-image/protected/unmatched-command/unreachable-mcp) ends with a legible instruction card naming the tool and why, never silent
a denied-tool pause routes to the setup-pause state and does not consume a retry/backoff attempt or dead-letter; a late approval resumes and reruns the job
the synchronous zero-timeout autonomous permission protocol is unchanged
items.outcome: Scheduled (autonomous) jobs no longer silently degrade when the agent reaches a tool it lacks. Every such denial is now terminal: a grantable one raises the one-tap approval card (approving grants the agent and, for an under-declared tool, adds it to the job) and the job retries; a non-grantable one ends with a legible instruction card naming the tool and why. Side effects are fenced after cancellation, the first parallel denial is sticky, grantability is carried authoritatively (spoof-proof), the requirement append runs only after the grant commits, and DeepAgents pre-check denials are terminal too (Ravi's 'fix once for good'). Decision 0115 amended; D-0051 resolved; D-0050 (cross-store atomicity) deferred. 8778 unit tests, verify.py, and a 5-round whole-branch autoreview all green.

items.story: As a teammate chatting with the agent, my turns in fully-synced conversations respond without waiting on redundant provider history fetches, so the agent feels immediate once it has everything.

items.outcome: Files shared in Discord now behave like Slack files. The agent saves the bytes the moment a file is posted, remembers the filename and where it came from, and can fetch an old file it never saved the first time someone needs it. When a message is deleted on Discord, its files are honestly reported as deleted and the stored bytes are removed — durably, so a deletion that races message ingestion, hits a transient database error, or arrives for a not-yet-stored message still lands. Ephemeral content is never stored, downloads only ever come from Discord's CDN with no credentials attached, and every file stays locked to its own conversation. Remaining edges (attachment removal via message edits, marker retention hygiene) are recorded as deferrals with triggers.

items.story: High audit finding: Telegram (fs.writeFile / open(path,'w')) and Slack (lstat-then-open race) attachment writers can follow a symlink out of the workspace and truncate a service-account-writable file. Reuse the descriptor-containment pattern already in workspace-message-attachment.ts (currently a reader). NOTE: Implementation exists unlanded in myclaw-SEC2 worktree (979264eb8): platform no-follow-fs + private-file-writer + Telegram/Slack wiring.

items.title: LLM passthrough: race-free concurrency admission + fewer body copies
items.story: High audit finding: /llm/v1/* has a per-minute counter but no concurrency semaphore, and buffers ≤16 MiB bodies several times (public read -> parse -> reserialize -> loopback -> gateway read). Acquire a race-free global and per-app/key concurrency permit BEFORE reading the body; reject excess before consuming bodies; release in one finally covering disconnect/parse/setup/provider failures. Reduce the body limit unless 16 MiB is justified. (Loopback collapse is the separate SIMP-3.)
acceptance_criteria: a global and per-app/key concurrency permit is acquired before body read; excess requests are rejected before body consumption
the permit is released in a single finally covering disconnect, parse failure, setup failure, provider failure, and streamed cleanup
barrier test: with upstream held, more-than-cap requests prove only the allowed number begin body consumption; RSS and open sockets measured under concurrent max-size requests
items.outcome: Shipped in SEC-1 / PR #280 (race-free LLM concurrency admission).

items.title: Ambient liveness (Part B)
items.story: As anyone waiting on the agent, I want honest ambient signals — a card that says it's still working when stalled, typing that stops lying, reactions that acknowledge my messages — without a single extra message in the conversation.
acceptance_criteria: 3-minute stall flips the existing progress card to plain 'Still working' (replace-only) and pauses typing; output resumes both
Discord TypingSink implemented; Slack stays truthfully sink-less
Seen->running reaction flip after ~5s without output, cleared on first output, on Slack/Telegram/Discord (first removeReaction implementations)
Accepted and deferred continuations both get a seen reaction at the single continuation seam
Retryable failures edit the same card ('retrying n/max'); only final failure finalizes it
Teams items deferred on the real-client trigger; goal-prompt doc Part B/C truth updated
items.outcome: Gantry now shows truthful, low-noise liveness in chats: typing indicators only while the agent is genuinely working, a single 'Still working' card edit if a turn stalls past 3 minutes, seen-to-running reaction flips on the triggering message, retry status on the same card, and receipts on both continuation routes. Under the hood, progress-card updates are strictly serialized per card with self-healing repair, so slow or failed Discord/Slack/Telegram API calls can no longer leave stale 'Still working' text, duplicate Stop buttons, or lost 'Done.' states.

items.title: Jobs: batch the latest-run projection (kill the list N+1)
items.story: High audit finding: GET /v1/jobs runs loadLatestRunsByJobId = Promise.all of one listJobRuns(job.id,1) per job (up to 500 concurrent). Add one batch repository method returning the latest run for all requested job IDs via DISTINCT ON (job_id) or a window function; build the visibility metadata synchronously from two maps. Subsumes the audit's simplification #4.
acceptance_criteria: a 500-job list issues a constant, small number of SQL queries (instrumented)
latest-run ordering, health/staleness, error summaries, app filtering, and the public response schema are unchanged
load test: concurrent list requests hold pool wait time and p95/p99 within target
items.outcome: Shipped on main as buildJobListVisibilityMetadata / listLatestJobRunsByJobIds (single batched query).

items.title: SSE: reserve the stream permit before subscription setup
items.story: Medium audit finding (TOCTOU): the session event-stream cap is checked before activeStreams is incremented after an await, so >25 concurrent setups all pass. Reserve/increment a token synchronously immediately after the check, before the first await; release it in one idempotent cleanup on setup failure/disconnect/close/normal end (mirror the sibling wait route). NOTE: overlaps CO-2 (coordination hardening TOCTOU batch) — land it there or here, not twice.
acceptance_criteria: the stream permit is reserved synchronously before the first await
barrier test: 26 concurrent requests admit exactly 25; the rest get 429 TOO_MANY_STREAMS; permits returned once on failure/disconnect
reconciled with CO-2 so the TOCTOU fix is not duplicated
items.outcome: Shipped in PERF-1 (c156cf9dd): SSE stream permits reserved before subscription setup.

items.title: Rate limits: cluster-authoritative store or declared singleton (decision required)
items.story: Medium audit finding: control + gateway rate limiters are per-process in-memory Maps, so the effective limit multiplies by replica count and resets on restart. Architecture decision required: enforce counters through one shared atomic store (Postgres/Redis) OR make the service singleton and reject horizontally-scaled config; document per-process vs cluster-wide for each limit. Record a decision before implementing.
acceptance_criteria: a decision record chooses shared-store vs declared-singleton and is accepted
two live replicas accept a combined count equal to the configured cluster limit (if shared-store) OR horizontally-scaled config is rejected (if singleton)
each limit documented as per-process or cluster-wide
items.outcome: Decided by record 0099: runtime is single-instance-authoritative for rate limits; cluster store deferred behind an explicit multi-instance revisit trigger. No code.

items.title: Live-admission: admission caps + terminal retention (decision required)
items.story: Medium audit finding: the durable live-admission table has no per-app/per-conversation admission cap at insert and no terminal retention (rows with identity metadata accumulate forever). Add atomic admission limits at the insert transaction returning an explicit overloaded/deferred outcome; define terminal retention with an ended_at index and a bounded purge/archival job. Architecture decision required and its retention half overlaps DUR-1 / deferral D-0001 — reconcile so retention is defined once.
acceptance_criteria: atomic per-app (and optionally per-conversation) admission cap; overload returns an explicit outcome; exact replay still returns the existing item
terminal retention defined with an ended_at-based index and a bounded purge that never removes active/deferred/recently-completed items
retention ownership reconciled with DUR-1 / D-0001 (defined once)
items.notes: Decision 0103 accepted 2026-08-03: 30-day TTL sweep of terminal rows via existing maintenance machinery. Remaining work is the sweep job + test.
items.outcome: Merged PR #378: 30-day TTL sweep of terminal live-admission rows (bounded advisory-locked batches from scheduler maintenance, 6h cadence, retry-on-failure). Completes PERF-4 with the earlier caps half.

items.title: Make check:architecture a required CI gate
items.story: Medium audit finding: check:architecture is a documented ratchet but absent from CI. PAY-1 already restored a green baseline (exit 0). Add the command as a required CI step; add a fixture/controlled mutation per rule class proving CI fails on one additional violation; baseline any accepted debt with exact path/count entries. Sequence with E2E-3 (the same make-a-green-checker-required move).
acceptance_criteria: check:architecture runs in ci.yml and a clean HEAD passes it
a controlled mutation per rule class proves CI fails on one added violation
expired/over-budget exceptions fail the gate
items.outcome: Branch protection enabled on main: the ci check (unit + integration + postgres + structural gates incl. check:architecture) is REQUIRED before merge; force-pushes and deletions blocked; enforce_admins off so the harness ledger keeps direct-push access.

items.title: Construct control application services once in the composition root
items.story: Audit simplification: createJobManagementService and createSessionInteractionModule are rebuilt per route from global getters. Build them once in the control-server composition root and pass through ControlRouteContext; keep live settings getters behind explicit getters so settings-reload behavior is unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: job and session services constructed once and injected via ControlRouteContext
live values (settings reload, app identity, credential broker, clocks, event exchange) still read live
route tests pass before and after settings reload and runtime-store init
items.outcome: Merged PR #377: JobManagementService and SessionInteractionModule constructed once in the control composition root; live deps via getters; liveAdmissionAppId is a method argument.

items.title: Provider content gaps: honest fallbacks, quick fixes, Slack canvas CRUD
items.story: Six verified quick fixes (honest binary fallback guidance, .eml text, Slack snippet delivery, Discord voice-note classification, Telegram location/venue/contact data, Discord embed folding) plus Slack canvas read/create/update behind host-issued handles with split read/write authority. Teams equivalents deferred to TEAMS-1; reading reactions/edits stays backlog.
acceptance_criteria: binary attachments return typed guidance, never truncated base64
Slack oversized messages deliver as snippet (<=1MB) or .txt file with text-path fallback on provider failure
canvas create/update/read tools enforce the split-capability trust boundary and IPC bounds per the plan
TEAMS-1 roadmap entry carries the deferred Teams criteria
items.outcome: Agents on Slack can now work with canvases: reading a shared canvas returns its text plus safe section handles, and agents can create a channel canvas or edit one section at a time (insert, replace, delete) with a confirmation step before wipe-and-replace. Every edit targets an exact Slack section id captured at read time, so a renamed or deleted section can never be silently overwritten; timeouts, deleted canvases and missing Slack scopes all come back as clear instructions instead of hangs. Slack app installs now list the extra scopes needed (files/canvases) and existing installs keep working with a warning until they are reinstalled. The vendored companion gate also got hardened along the way: the read-only exploration lane is now a provable grammar instead of a text scan.

items.title: Safe Web UI foundation shell
items.story: As a Gantry maintainer, I can validate a disconnected web shell without changing the hosted runtime or its delivery artifacts.
acceptance_criteria: apps/web builds independently under /ui and renders a responsive accessible Not connected shell with local preferences
separate root and CI commands validate web formatting, typecheck, lint and build
the production build does not create or copy dist/ui and runtime serving, APIs, auth, storage, providers and Docker remain unchanged
architecture docs state the source-only boundary and require a later approved integration PR

items.title: Provider-aware tool surface: affinity-filtered projection + dynamic per-provider instructions
items.value: Agents only see tools that work on their conversation's provider, and their instructions explain exactly how shared tools behave there (split thresholds, rich-render shapes, option caps). Cleaner tool lists, fewer wasted turns, a declared checklist for future providers.
acceptance_criteria: canvas_* absent from Telegram/Discord/unknown-provider tool surfaces in BOTH the spawn projection and the runner-process parse path; present for Slack incl. jobs-lane spawns
affinity beats explicit GANTRY_CONFIGURED_ALLOWED_TOOLS_JSON entries
each provider's compiled system prompt carries its own tool guidance built from imported limit constants, and no other provider's
docs/architecture/tool-provider-affinity.md records the full tool classification
items.outcome: Agents now only see the tools that actually work where they are: Slack agents keep the canvas tools, while Telegram, Discord and other conversations no longer carry three dead tools they could never use — enforced in both the spawn projection and inside the runner process, and even an operator config entry cannot re-add a tool that cannot function there. Each agent's instructions now also explain, per provider, how its shared tools behave: where long messages split, how rich cards degrade, how many question options fit — with every number imported from the real code constants so the guidance can never drift. A classification of all 75 tools plus a checklist for wiring future providers landed in docs/architecture.

items.title: Physical attachment hand-off for ALL providers: materialize conversation files into the agent workspace
items.story: An attachment_materialize tool copies a conversation-scoped attachment (host-issued ref, signed proof — the attachment_open trust model) into a quarantined subdirectory of the agent's CURRENT workspace, size-capped, on explicit request, so agents can process files with any tool (scripts over CSVs, proper conversions, native model PDF/image reads, re-upload of results). Requires its own decision record: crossing the deliberate workspace/attachment-store isolation, with the quarantine contract (dedicated dir, never auto-read into context, prompt guidance that contents are untrusted data not instructions). Provider-neutral by construction: operates on the shared provider-attachments store, so Slack, Telegram, and Discord are covered identically at ship time and Teams inherits automatically when FILE-1C Graph capture lands. Decision 0105 (accepted) holds the quarantine contract. Generalizes the native-PDF hand-off follow-up recorded during PR #379.
acceptance_criteria: decision record for the workspace-boundary crossing and quarantine contract, accepted before implementation
attachment_materialize mints only from conversation-scoped host-issued refs; size-capped; writes only inside the quarantine dir via the hardened writer
quarantined files are reachable by agent tools but never auto-ingested into context; prompt guidance marks them untrusted data
models with pdfInput/imageInput can be handed the physical file where the runner supports it
materialization verified for a Slack, a Telegram, and a Discord attachment through the same code path (no provider branches)
items.outcome: Agents can now get the real file, not just a text view: a new attachment_materialize tool copies one conversation attachment at a time into a quarantine folder inside the agent's own workspace, so scripts, converters and capable models can work on the actual bytes. Every copy is explicit, capped at 50 MB, cryptographically tied to the conversation it came from, written through the hardened writer that refuses symlink tricks, and logged. Files Telegram already dropped into the workspace are answered honestly with their existing path instead of a duplicate copy, and a stale reference falls back to re-fetching from the provider. The agent's instructions mark the quarantine folder as untrusted data to process with tools, never instructions to follow.

items.title: Collapse the direct-LLM loopback HTTP hop into one in-process service
items.story: Audit simplification (pairs with SEC-3): the direct API path serializes and buffers the same request through two in-process HTTP layers (public route -> loopback -> model gateway). Extract provider forwarding into one in-process application operation used directly by the public route; keep the loopback HTTP adapter only for child runners that need an HTTP endpoint. Do after SEC-3's concurrency admission lands.
acceptance_criteria: the direct API path no longer makes a loopback HTTP hop; one body reader and one serialize/deserialize cycle removed
provider credential isolation, per-app/route audit, provider path confinement, streaming, cancellation, rate limits, and child-runner gateway support unchanged
contract test: identical provider URL/headers/body/frames/usage/errors/cancellation before and after

items.title: Make durable coordination mandatory; remove process-local fallbacks
items.story: Audit simplification: AsyncTaskRepository atomic admission/claim are optional, and session compaction falls back to a process-global Set when the durable method is absent — two coordination systems with different guarantees. Make atomic admission/claim required for production repositories; the in-memory test repository implements the same atomic semantics. Removes createTaskWithLocalAdmission, optional-method probing, and the global compaction dedup set. Overlaps DUR-1 — fold in unless it lands sooner as standalone cleanup.
acceptance_criteria: atomic admission/claim required; local count/create and global compaction-dedup fallbacks removed
per-app/per-agent backlog caps, compaction dedup, stale-task recovery, fencing, and restart-safe records unchanged
concurrent admission tests pass against Postgres and the in-memory repository (two workers, restart, stale tasks, cap boundaries)
reconciled with DUR-1 (not implemented twice)

items.title: Liveness hardening: unified dispatcher, declared capabilities, deterministic tests
items.story: As a chat user, I always see truthful liveness signals (reactions, typing, progress) while the agent works, so that I never wonder whether it heard me
acceptance_criteria: Adapters declare liveness in one liveUx capability object; no advertised no-ops (Teams reactions: none, Slack typing: none)
One route-aware dispatcher owns reaction/typing delivery: bounded deadlines, catch-and-warn, rate-limit warn+retry-once, loud missing-sink diagnosis; a liveness failure can never fail a turn
One liveness phase owner; reaction admission and terminal restore share one scope; first-reaction send cannot block the turn; typing resumes on stall recovery
Provider fixes land: Telegram replace-only/flip/topic-typing, Slack restart stale-and-repost, Discord thread-reaction fallback removal, batch backwards-scan, flip-race settlement
Proven-dead state deleted (3 dedupe registries, unreachable rollback, unused alias map); tombstone collapse deferred as D-0043
Liveness suites assert final provider-visible state via a shared stateful fake with failure/latency/restart falsifiers; flow-level chain test; two-account sink tests
items.outcome: Ambient liveness now behaves the same way everywhere. Each chat app declares honestly what it can do (Slack has no typing; Teams cannot react), one dispatcher delivers every reaction and typing signal with the same rules — bounded waits, loud logs, provider-respecting backoff, self-correction when a slow request lands late — and one controller owns a turn's liveness end to end, so signals are never stranded, typing resumes after a stall, and a liveness failure cannot kill a turn. The bugs behind the missed emojis are fixed across Telegram, Slack, Discord and batch turns. The tests that let this ship broken were rebuilt around a stateful fake provider that can fail and stall, asserting what a user would actually see.

items.title: Attachment failures say which cause: actionable copy, per-cause logs, honest doctor
items.story: As someone sharing a file with the agent, when it can't read the file I am told what went wrong and what would fix it, so that I am not stuck guessing
acceptance_criteria: Each failure cause (permission_scope, not_a_member/not_visible, deleted, too_large, rate_limited, timeout, transport) produces its own plain-English, actionable sentence; unknown is the only path to the legacy generic copy
Every classified failure logs once at warn with cause, provider, providerAccountId, conversationJid, attachmentId, provider status where present, and elapsed ms — and no token, URL or file bytes

The two host-side silent paths gain logs (resolver deadline and incapable routing); the runner no-response timeout gets timeout-specific user copy only, its host log deferred to D-0045 because the runner lacks the account context and application logger
A Slack token missing files:read yields a named doctor warning that survives aggregation (naming the scope and the reinstall step) while the check still passes
The reported scenario — files:read missing, every file type — yields the permission sentence plus exactly one permission_scope log line
items.outcome: When Gantry can't open a file someone shared, it now says why in plain language and tells them what to do — 'the app needs the files:read permission; ask an admin to reinstall Gantry', 'that file was deleted', 'the channel is rate-limiting requests, try again in a few minutes', instead of one vague 'I can't get that file right now' for every case. Operators get exactly one diagnostic log per failure, tagged with the specific cause (and the HTTP status when there is one), and the setup doctor now warns loudly when a Slack install is missing files:read instead of passing silently. So a person hitting the reported bug — every Slack file failing with a generic message and no logs — now sees the actual reason and the fix.

items.title: Legacy clean-cut: single canonical shape, delete compat readers
items.story: As a maintainer, I want every runtime read path to accept only the one canonical data shape (legacy inputs rejected or reset, never silently migrated), so the codebase honors decision 0003 and job/permission/settings/memory state is auditable.
acceptance_criteria: No runtime read path runs a legacy migration or ownership reconstruction: migrateLegacyAgentBindings, the jobs JID/default-app/sessionId-empty path, and the skill remote-missing->local fallback are gone (greppable + tests)

Legacy inputs are rejected with a clear error or ignored, never silently migrated: settings agents.*.bindings -> remediation error; memory malformed snapshot -> fail closed; skill remote-missing -> fail closed; permission null-request branch deleted
One canonical shape per domain: single providerAccount field+prefix; a JobOwner discriminator; review_snapshot_json NOT NULL
Live gantry data handled per migrate/reset (migrate jobs; reset settings bindings, memory-review nulls, thread:slack ids) and the runtime boots green after migration
Dead/duplicate surface removed: ./primitives export, provider CLI info/control-allowlist aliases, thread:slack: parser, runAgent prod-type optionality, brain-review optionality
check:architecture rejects a new compat branch (silent migration/dual-read/ownership-reconstruction/remote-to-local fallback) lacking a time-boxed exception record, and is green for this change
verify.py green; one 3-lens branch autoreview clean; no legacy-preserving test remains
items.outcome: Every runtime read path now accepts one canonical data shape and nothing else. Legacy-shaped data is rejected with a clear remediation message or ignored — never silently rewritten — so disk and code agree and each area stays auditable. Settings with obsolete agent bindings are refused with reset-and-reimport instructions; a missing memory-review snapshot, a skill artifact the remote says is gone, and a malformed permission request all fail safe instead of trusting stale or fabricated data; dead surface (a duplicate export, two provider CLI aliases, an old Slack thread-id parser, test-only seams) is deleted. A new check:architecture guardrail stops these shortcuts creeping back without a dated, owned exception. The providerConnection rename and job-ownership cuts are deferred.

items.title: Scheduled runs use granted capability-backed commands; pause with one clear message
items.story: As a job owner, I want my scheduled job to actually use the tools and capabilities I granted it and to get one clear message when it needs my help, so that it completes its work instead of silently stalling and I am not spammed with duplicate technical cards.
acceptance_criteria: A scheduled run whose agent is granted a semantic capability (with its reviewed definition) can invoke that capability's command without denial; an ungranted capability still denies legibly.
Canonical capabilities like Browser keep working (regression).
One denied-tool pause emits exactly one plain-language user notification with no duplicate terminal card, and a one-tap approve when the denial is grantable.
items.outcome: Scheduled jobs can now actually use the tools and capabilities you granted them. A scheduled run that reaches a command its agent is host-granted (like the gog Google Sheets commands) now asks the host coordinator to authorize it instead of dead-ending — so the job does its work instead of stalling — while the settings denylist stays a hard, un-overridable boundary and the agent still can't self-grant (PERM-2 preserved; decision 0116). And a job that genuinely must pause now sends you ONE plain-language message ("This job paused because it couldn't use X. Needed: …") instead of three overlapping technical cards. Codex validated the root cause read-only; 8781 unit tests, verify.py, and a whole-branch autoreview all green. One cosmetic edge case deferred (D-0052).

items.title: Scheduled jobs declare tools upfront (neutral) + grantable setup cards
items.story: As a job owner, I want scheduled jobs to be set up with the tools they need and to grant any missing tool in one tap, so my jobs run without dead-end pauses.
acceptance_criteria: Ungranted builtin facade tools show a one-tap grant button on the setup card, both lanes; tap grants the canonical selection + appends the canonical job requirement.
Scheduling a job whose task needs an ungranted tool declares it and yields an actionable card shortly after creation; a job needing only granted tools is ready with no card.
No duplicate card (existing fingerprint dedup); passive setup event retained; behaviour identical across both runner lanes; no prime/runMode introduced.
items.outcome: Scheduled jobs are now set up with the tools they need, and setup pauses are actionable. When a scheduled run needs a builtin tool it wasn't granted (web search/read, file read/write, browser), the Setup-needed card now shows a one-tap Allow-for-future button instead of a dead-end message, on both runner lanes, so the owner grants it from chat; the grant persists the canonical selection and adds it to the job requirements. When an agent schedules a job it now declares the tools the task needs, so a missing tool surfaces as one actionable card shortly after creation (dispatched async, so creating stays fast) rather than only when a run later pauses. Jobs whose tools are all granted run with no pause. Authority stays host-reviewed and human-approved (no agent self-grant).

items.title: Person-scoped grants and kind-aware approval authority
items.story: As anyone talking to the agent, I can approve my agent's tool requests right where I'm talking to it, and a permission I grant in my DM stays private to me and never leaks to other people or shared rooms, so approvals are actionable on every provider without silently widening a shared assistant's access.
acceptance_criteria: In a 1:1 DM the DM's own user can approve a setup/permission card with no allowlist entry; a non-participant cannot; groups still require an allowlisted approver.

A durable grant approved in one person's DM is used only when the agent acts for that person, never for another DM or a group on the same agent; existing grants keep applying as shared with no regression.
A job created in a DM uses that person's grants at run time; a job created in a group uses shared grants; the scope a setup-card grant lands in is the scope the job runs in.
A durable DM self-grant is permitted only for a personal-memory-eligible person; others may approve for the current run only.

Installing the bot into a new group by a recognised person seeds that person as the first approver with an in-group acknowledgement, on every provider where the installer is identifiable; behaviour is uniform across providers with no per-provider approval logic.
items.outcome: Tool grants are now person-scoped where a person exists. In a 1:1 DM the user can approve their own agent's permission requests without being pre-listed, and an 'allow for future' they grant stays private to them instead of widening the shared assistant for every chat. Groups keep the explicit approver allowlist and shared grants. Scheduled jobs inherit the identity of the conversation that created them: a DM-created job's durable grant is written for that person (an unresolvable job fails closed rather than widening to shared); group jobs stay shared. The acting person is simply the memory identity, host-stamped onto the request - the elaborate trust machinery built en route was removed per the accepted 0118 tradeoff. Installer group-onboarding split to PSCOPE-2.

items.title: Provider-neutral installer auto-seed and in-group acknowledgement
items.story: As the person who installs the agent into a group, I am seeded as its first approver and the group is told so, so that approvals work out of the box without manual allowlist setup
acceptance_criteria: Installing the bot into a new group by a recognised person seeds that person as the first approver and posts an in-group acknowledgement
An unrecognised installer seeds nobody; the group gets a clear message on how to set an approver (fail-closed)
Only installer-id extraction is per-provider; behaviour degrades to manual where the installer is unidentifiable
items.outcome: Adding the bot to a group is no longer dead air, and groups can finally bootstrap their first approver. When someone the bot already knows from a 1:1 chat adds it to a Telegram group or Slack channel, the group registers itself, that person becomes its first approver, and the bot says so in the room. Anyone the bot does not recognise gets a clear in-group message naming how to set an approver - and nothing else (fail-closed). Discord posts the same guidance once per new server; Teams stays documented-manual. The old Telegram DM Yes/No flow - which could never mint a first approver and never spoke in the group - is deleted. Approvals themselves are unchanged: the allowlist still governs groups.

items.title: Structured invocation for local-CLI capabilities
items.story: As an operator running scheduled jobs that use CLI capabilities, I want the agent to invoke them structurally instead of authoring shell, so benign output-bounding never terminally fails the run
acceptance_criteria: A granted local_cli capability runs via a structured tool with no shell string, no classifier consult, bounded output; unreviewed subcommands/flags/excess args are rejected
Execution reuses the existing sandbox + output-boundary + timeout/cancellation and verifies the executable identity at invocation
At cutover the RunCommand projection no longer authorizes these capabilities and existing scheduled jobs invoke via the structured path
items.outcome: Local-CLI capabilities (gog/sheets) are now invoked structurally instead of the agent hand-writing shell. The agent calls capability_run with the capability id and an argument list; the host validates the argv arity-exactly against the reviewed template, verifies the executable in place, and runs it in the existing sandbox with bounded output. No shell string exists, so pipes/redirects/chaining/globs are impossible, authorization is the deterministic granted-capability check (no flaky classifier, no autonomous terminal denial), and the RunCommand projection is retired so no shell fallback remains. This closes the class that paused KnackLabs on gog|head, for any CLI. Deep executable-identity hardening is deferred (D-0056).

items.title: Autonomous runs decide permissions deterministically — no classifier
items.story: As an operator, my scheduled jobs never pause on a tool the job already has — the same call gets the same decision every run, and only a genuinely undeclared tool produces the one grantable pause card.
acceptance_criteria: No autonomous-run permission decision is made by the classifier (decidedBy=auto_classifier never appears with a jobId run)
A tool in the job's effective allowed tools always matches the autonomous matcher (granted implies matched)
send_message to the run's own conversation/thread is deterministically allowed when granted; other destinations terminally deny with the grantable card
Ungranted tool on an autonomous run: terminal deny + existing pause card, no classifier invocation
Granting from the pause card resumes the job automatically; the re-run uses the grant and completes without re-asking (fix-and-continue proven end to end)
items.outcome: Scheduled jobs no longer live or die by a model's mood. An autonomous run's tool permissions are now a pure function of what the job was granted: a granted tool always runs, an ungranted one pauses the job once with a single grant card, and tapping Allow resumes the job permanently - the same call gets the same answer every run. The classifier that used to coin-flip these decisions (45 lucky allows, 15 dead jobs in the logs, including the KnackLabs send_message pause) now serves interactive chats only, where a human can actually answer its ask. Decision 0121 pins the contract; the whole loop is proven end to end on live Postgres.

items.title: Capability template amendment via grantable card
items.story: As an operator, when a CLI capability's approved command shape doesn't fit reality, I get one plain-language card in chat — approve it and the blocked job fixes itself and continues; I never touch SQL or restart anything.
acceptance_criteria: HISTORICAL (superseded by decision 0125): agent-raised amendment proposal on template mismatch (new request_access target kind); proposals are review metadata, never self-applying

Card is plain-language: ability-terms body from displayName/can/cannot, one-sentence warning when the delta widens ability, technical detail collapsed; no template strings, argv, ids, or hashes in the body
Human approval updates the durable capability definition with provenance (who, when, prior templates in history); deny is terminal and deduped for the same template/argv pair
Amendment covers commandTemplates only; hash/path/version attempts through this surface are rejected
Live proof: the KnackLabs sheets mismatch is fixed from the card and the next run writes leads - no SQL, no restart
items.outcome: When a CLI capability's approved command shape doesn't fit how the command really works, the agent now asks for a fix instead of failing forever: one plain-language card lands in chat - what stopped, what approving changes, what the capability still can and cannot do - with Approve fix / Deny buttons and the technical delta collapsed behind them. Approving updates the reviewed definition once, with full provenance and history, and every job blocked on that capability resumes and completes without re-asking. Denying is final for that definition; timeouts just ask again later. The KnackLabs sheets breakage is this feature's live acceptance test: fixing it becomes one tap instead of SQL.

items.title: Capability executable update via grantable card
items.story: As an operator, upgrading a CLI tool never silently kills my jobs: one card tells me the tool was updated, I tap Trust update, and everything that uses it resumes.
acceptance_criteria: executable_identity_mismatch raises one host-verified update proposal per executable (agent claims never trusted; host measures the on-disk binary)
Card is plain-language with version framing; Trust update / Deny; hashes and paths only in the collapsed technical view
Approval CAS-updates identity for every capability pinned to that executable in one tap; templates untouched; provenance + prior identity in history
Deny is terminal per (path, observed hash) until the binary changes again; timeouts stay pending and redispatch; blocked jobs resume on approval (fix-and-continue)

items.title: Every pause card carries a real action
items.story: As an operator, no job ever pauses into a dead end: every setup card offers at least one button - approve the exact scoped command it tried, approve the capability fix, or another concrete action - never prose alone.
items.outcome: Paused scheduled jobs are no longer dead ends: every pause/setup message now arrives with working buttons on Slack, Telegram, Discord and Teams. A job paused for a blocked shell command offers 'Allow once for this run' — one more run that asks live for that exact command, nothing permanently granted — and 'Pause job', which now really pauses the job from the card on every provider (it used to be guidance text). Double taps, crashed taps and concurrent taps all collapse into exactly one extra run.

items.title: Seamless scheduled-job lifecycle: typed denials, durable approval cards, host-filed fixes
items.story: As a job owner, when my scheduled job hits a blocker I always get an actionable card I can tap - never a silent stall - and recognized fixes are filed for my approval automatically
acceptance_criteria: Every terminal autonomous denial in scope is typed and observable (event, status, visibility)
A setup pause produces a card with working buttons, with bounded delivery and defined recovery for ambiguous, expired, exhausted, and cancelled outcomes
A recognized capability template mismatch yields a host-compiled fix-proposal card; owner approval applies both templates and durably resumes the job
Job prompts carry business logic only; the KnackLabs prompt sweep is completed inside the live acceptance gate
Live gate passes on the real KnackLabs job in the owner's Telegram, including the crash/restart fault matrix

items.title: Prefix-wildcard CLI-command capability permissions (delete the widening machinery)
items.story: As an autonomous agent, I can run any invocation under a capability's reviewed command PREFIX (flags and values included) with no per-shape negotiation, so a safe CLI operation never dead-ends and never needs a hand-patch — the reviewed executable + literal operation prefix is the security boundary, arguments within it are unbounded (Claude Code's Bash(<prefix>:*) model).
acceptance_criteria: A held capability's reviewed template authorizes any invocation matching its executable + literal operation prefix, flags included: a terminal standalone * is the reviewed argv remainder; ONE shared matcher governs dry-run auth, execution, AND compiler coverage; no legacy exact-arity mode (decision 0129)

The prefix is a hard boundary: executable + literal operation prefix match exactly; a non-terminal * is exactly one non-flag arg (no flag injection, including mixed globs); shell-control/redirection/environment-assignment templates are refused

mcp__gantry__capability_run auto-allow is DISPATCH-ONLY: the runner may only hand a schema-valid envelope to the host which re-authorizes; the bypass grants NO command authority; capability_run stays HIGH-risk with no classifier-derived or cached allow (decision 0130)
An already-covered call records no amendment and resumes; a genuine uncovered prefix still asks once (mismatch -> proposal -> approve -> durable intent -> resume); denial is terminal

Acceptance: the end-to-end loop is proven on the real Postgres integration lane, with a comma-containing --values-json payload preserved byte-for-byte (the KnackLabs live write is owner-run after merge)

Stats are accurate and neutral across both the Anthropic SDK and deepagents runtimes (final heartbeat snapshot on stop; browserActivityCount reflects a confirmed browser action, not just prelaunch)

The card renders natively per provider (Telegram HTML, Slack Block Kit, Discord embed) via a typed jobNotificationView, with the neutral markdown string as fallback for persistence and unsupported channels

items.title: Deterministic structured job result from recorded run actions
items.story: As an operator, I want a scheduled job's completion notification to show what it actually did (capabilities run, browser actions, failures) derived deterministically from recorded run actions, so that I see the real outcome instead of raw truncated narration.
acceptance_criteria: Scheduled capability_run success emits a run-scoped record (capabilityId + outcome, args opt-in gated + redacted) so the outcome is queryable at completion

items.outcome: Every scheduled job (and every live turn) now produces a structured, neutral summary of what it actually did for any tool on either runtime and provider - grouped actions with counts, failed-first, family-aware labels (e.g. 'Google Sheets Values Append x3', 'WebSearch x5', 'Browser: Open') - instead of falling back to raw narration. A single tool.activity event is recorded per tool call on both worker runtimes and both inline lanes with per-invocation correlation; Gantry-owned capability/browser events dedup against the generic event via trusted, provenance-gated result metadata (decision 0133), so a third-party tool can never spoof correlation. Someone reading a finished job now sees exactly which actions ran and which failed.

acceptance_criteria: Unmatched grantable tool call raises the standard card; authorized Allow resumes the SAME run in place; rule persists; next run silent-allows; unit+live

The job notification was rebuilt alongside it: exactly one message per run, edited from Running into the result, rendered natively on Telegram, Slack and Discord, leading with a one-line outcome, then the per-tool results, then the next run time. Operators also got a heredoc-aware command gate, honest 'this request stays open' wording on job prompts, and the KnackLabs incident class (one card edited ten thousand times) is closed by JSONB-faithful settlement.

items.title: Channel dispatchers: flatten repeated guards and split the Telegram callback by action kind
items.story: As a maintainer, I read the Telegram message-action dispatcher as small per-action handlers and the provider adapters without repeated optional-guard chains, so that changes stay reviewable and the biggest hotspot from the JOBPERM-1 review is retired.
acceptance_criteria: The five review hoists are applied: telegram/message-action-affordances.ts dead early-returns removed; telegram/channel-connect.ts callback context computed once; slack/channel-message-action-handler.ts channelId/userId hoisted; discord/interactions.ts component user id hoisted; teams/cards.ts thread fragment computed once

The Telegram bot.on callback in telegram/channel-connect.ts is split by action kind into named handlers, each with cyclomatic complexity <= 25, dispatched from a callback whose own complexity is <= 15; no behaviour change
No behaviour change: existing unit tests pass unchanged (only new tests may be added); tsc, architecture check, unit + Postgres integration lanes green
Lands after PR #446 merged (CHAN-1 folder layout); branch based on main after it
items.outcome: The provider adapters are easier to read and change safely. Five repeated guards (Telegram, Slack, Discord, Teams) are computed once instead of per branch, and the Telegram callback — previously one ~700-line function handling every button tap — is now a thin dispatcher that builds one context object and hands each kind of tap (question answers, stop, job-permission card, memory/brain reviews, observer, retry, classic permission prompt) to a named handler in its own module. Nothing changed in behaviour: every existing test passes untouched. Complexity: dispatcher 11, largest handler 16 (ceilings 15/25).

AC2: Allow on a once row replays a signed allow_once to the runner, writes no rule, and the held tool call resumes; Deny denies; the card settles and logs delivery as today
AC3: rule rows behave exactly as before; existing rows without a mode read as rule
AC4: a job attach failure denies the tool call with a logged plain reason instead of falling through to the chat prompt

items.title: Job runner: split runActiveJob and runQuery by phase

acceptance_criteria: runActiveJob in jobs/execution.ts is split by phase into named functions in ONE sibling module, each with cyclomatic complexity <= 25, sequenced from a body whose own complexity is <= 15; no behaviour change

runQuery in runner/query-loop.ts is split by phase into named functions in ONE sibling module, each with cyclomatic complexity <= 25, driven from a loop body whose own complexity is <= 15; no behaviour change
No behaviour change: existing unit and Postgres integration tests pass unchanged (only new tests may be added); tsc, architecture check, unit + Postgres integration lanes green
Branch based on main after PR #451 (CHAN-2)
items.outcome: The two biggest functions in the runtime are now readable one phase at a time. The job run loop (runActiveJob, 733 lines in one body) and the SDK query loop (runQuery, ~600 lines) each became a short sequencer over one context object, with every phase a named function in sibling modules — setup/lease/agent/finalization for jobs, options/setup and one handler per message kind for the query loop. Nothing changed in behaviour: every existing unit and Postgres integration test passes untouched. Complexity on the AST counter: sequencers under 15, largest phase under 25 (ceilings 15/25).

items.title: Remove the providerConnection dual-read
items.story: As a maintainer, settings and control code read provider accounts through one name only, so the 19 expired architecture exceptions disappear and the architecture gate is green on main again.
acceptance_criteria: AC1: the providerConnection shadow field is removed from the runtime settings types and the parser no longer fills it; every providerAccount ?? providerConnection read collapses to providerAccount (settings parser/validation/renderer/exports/reconcile/observer activation, control-plane storage model, CLI provider utils, Slack permission delivery, control routes).
AC2: a settings document that still carries providerConnection / provider_connection is ignored silently — the key is dropped on read and provider_account is the only source; nothing dual-reads it.
AC3: the 19 providerConnection entries are deleted from scripts/architecture-exceptions.json and npm run check:architecture passes with no providerConnection exception.
AC4: existing unit and Postgres integration suites pass (only assertions that named providerConnection change); tsc green.
items.outcome: The old providerConnection name no longer lives anywhere in the runtime settings path: the in-memory shadow field and its parser fill are gone, every providerAccount ?? providerConnection read now reads provider accounts only, writers stop creating the property, and the 19 expired architecture exceptions are deleted, so npm run check:architecture is green on main again. Behaviour is unchanged: a settings document that still says provider_connection keeps being rejected by the existing strict key check (now covered by a test), and the Slack approver lookup stays account-qualified. providerConnectionId and the missing_provider_connection enum are deliberately left alone (deferral D-0070).

items.title: Settled job permission cards disappear like chat prompts
items.story: As the owner of a scheduled job, an answered permission card goes away the way an approved chat prompt does, so the group is not left with stale 'settled' cards after every run.
acceptance_criteria: AC1: when every row of a job permission card is settled by Allow, the card message is deleted on Telegram, Discord and Slack and edited to a one-line approved receipt on Teams; a failed delete falls back to the receipt edit
AC2: when any row is denied or expired, the card is edited to a one-line receipt per denied/expired request ('Permission denied: <command>' / 'Expired: <command>') on every provider — never deleted
AC3: the retire outcome (allowed | denied) is carried on the card revision by the shared projection; provider deliveries act on it; retry of a retire revision is idempotent
AC4: existing unit and Postgres integration suites pass (only new or updated assertions on the retire text/operation); tsc, architecture check green
items.outcome: Answered job permission cards now behave like chat prompts. When every request on a card is allowed, the card is deleted on Telegram, Slack and Discord (with a short approved receipt if the delete fails), and on Teams it becomes a one-line receipt card with no buttons. Requests that expired show as 'Expired: <command>' lines instead of lingering buttons; a denied request still keeps its live card row with one-tap Reconsider, as decision 0144 requires. The shared card record carries the retire outcome and the delete/receipt markers, so a retried delivery never deletes or edits twice and a recorded marker can never be rewritten. The Postgres once-card test now runs like a live job (delivered card, scheduler slot held), which is what exposed the ordering bug behind the earlier hang.
